name: Mama Cocha Effigy
powers: Gains the protection of the mother of the sea.
description: Mama Cocha, the mother of the sea, was counted among the great Inca divinities, the wife and sister of the creator god Viracocha and the mother of Inti the sun and Mama Killa the moon. Fisherfolk along the Pacific coast made offerings of shells and small carved images, and poured maize beer into the waves, and colonial chroniclers record that the goddess was honored among the household and regional deities of the empire, receiving her share at the great festivals. Her image in miniature, worn as an amulet or set at the shore, carried her protection onto the boats that worked her waters, calming storms and guiding the catch. Though the Inca state collapsed, the cult of the sea mother survived in coastal communities, where she is sometimes said to ride the currents still and to reward the faithful with a full net. The effigies are the tangible trace of that devotion, small objects that held an ocean in the mind of an empire.
source: Colonial chronicles of Inca religion and coastal offerings

name: Pachamanca
material: Heated stones dug into the earth
powers: Feeds the community and returns its first taste to the earth.
description: The pachamanca is an Andean feast cooked in the earth: stones are heated in a dug pit, and layers of meat, potatoes, maize, beans and fragrant herbs are set over them, covered with leaves and earth, and steamed until done. The name comes from Quechua and means 'earth pot,' and the method is shared across the Peruvian and Bolivian highlands, where it is served at weddings, patronal fiestas, harvests and the raising of a new house. Before anyone eats, the first portion is set aside and offered to Pachamama, the earth mother, often with a splash of chicha or a libation poured on the ground, a gesture of return for what the land gave. Regional variants distinguish the cooking of the sierra from the coastal pachamanca a la olla, and the dish has become a badge of Andean identity even as families adapt it to modern stoves. The offering that opens the feast keeps alive the old understanding that eating from the earth demands giving back to it first.
source: Andean oral tradition and contemporary practice

name: Mate Gourd
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Shared in a circle that marks friendship and trust.
description: The mate gourd is the dried calabash cup from which yerba mate, the leafy infusion of the Guaraní, is drunk through a metal straw called a bombilla, passed hand to hand around a circle of friends. The Guaraní of Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina prepared a drink of the herb before the Spanish arrived, and colonial accounts already describe it being shared; the Spanish word mate itself comes from the Quechua mati, for the gourd that holds it. Etiquette is precise: the cebador pours, drinks the first, often bitter, sip and refills, and the gourd circles clockwise, never returning to the cebador for a second serving until it has passed everyone. To drink from another's gourd is an act of trust and closeness, which is why the sharing of mate is still the everyday gesture of friendship in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Modern gourds are carved and sometimes rimmed with metal, but the meaning is unchanged: one gourd, many hands, a shared breath.
source: Guaraní tradition and colonial accounts of mate

name: Bolas
material: Balls of stone or iron joined by braided hide cords
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Entangles the legs of running cattle or game.
description: The bolas, or boleadoras, are throwing weights of the South American plains: two or three stone or iron balls, often covered in hide, joined by braided cords of leather. The hunter or gaucho swings them overhead and releases them to wrap around the legs of fleeing cattle, horses or rheas, tangling the animal in an instant fall. The weapon was developed by the Indigenous peoples of the Pampas and Patagonia and adopted wholesale by the colonial herders, and chroniclers recorded its use among the Mapuche and Tehuelche; a heavier solid type, the bolas perdidas, was hurled at enemies in war. The gaucho made the bolas his own, and the tool became so identified with him that it appears throughout the gauchesque literature, most famously in José Hernández's epic poem Martín Fierro. Today it survives in the cattle country of Argentina and Uruguay, used by the last horse-riding vaqueanos and kept alive as a symbol of the pampas.
source: Pampas tradition and colonial accounts

name: Kultrún
powers: Carries the heartbeat of the land into ceremony.
description: The kultrún is the sacred drum of the Mapuche of Chile and Argentina, a shallow wooden bowl covered with a hide head and beaten with a single stick or by hand, played almost exclusively by the machi, the ritual specialist and healer. Its head is painted with a quartered design, a cross and the four directions, which orients the ceremony and maps the structure of the Mapuche universe, and around it the ngillatun ceremony of prayer and thanks is built. The machi sounds the kultrún to summon the spirits, to guide healing rites called machitun, and to call the community into a single rhythm; the drum is so closely tied to the office that a machi's calling is said to announce itself partly through the drum. The instrument is treated with the respect owed a sacred object, carried into the center of the ceremonial circle and held close by its keeper. In the twenty-first century the kultrún remains central to Mapuche religious life and has also become a symbol of Indigenous identity and resistance in Chile.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Rewe
material: Carved wooden post with notched steps
powers: Ladder by which the machi climbs to speak with the spirits.
description: The rewe is the carved altar pole of the Mapuche, a notched wooden post raised in the ceremonial ground and in front of the machi's home, its steps climbed by the machi during rituals to draw close to the upper world of the spirits. The notches are a ladder, and the rewe is understood as the axis linking the worlds, planted at the point where the sacred and the human meet; it is often topped with carved figures of the beings or animals that guide the machi. Each machi's rewe is raised with ceremony, receives offerings and chants, and marks the ritual space where the community gathers for the ngillatun, the great ceremony of thanks and petition. The rewe is so emblematic of the machi's office that it is read as the symbol of Mapuche spirituality, and contemporary Mapuche communities still erect and tend their rewes. It stands as a living sign that the sacred is not far away but planted in the very ground of the ceremonial field.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Saci's Red Cap
aliases: The Cap of the One-Legged Imp
era: Brazilian folk tradition to the present
powers: Whoever wins it gains the Saci's power.
description: The red cap of the Saci is the knitted head covering of the most famous figure of Brazilian folklore, the one-legged spirit Saci-Pererê, who smokes a pipe, whistles through the dark, and raises whirlwinds along the roads. The cap is the seat of his power, and the tales hold that whoever can catch him and take the cap wins the Saci's obedience or his magic, a prize that always slips away, because the trickster escapes as soon as the cap is grabbed. In some versions the color changes, with the red-capped Saci of the paths joined by variants wearing green or other colored caps, each with its own mischief. Monteiro Lobato's stories of the early twentieth century fixed the image of the pipe-smoking, red-capped trickster in the national imagination, though the figure long predates him in Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous legend. The cap alone identifies the Saci in folk art, carnival costumes and children's books, making it one of the most recognizable objects of Brazilian folk culture.
source: Brazilian oral tradition and Monteiro Lobato's tales

name: Supay Figurine
powers: Opens the door to the world beneath the earth.
description: Supay is the lord of the uku pacha, the world beneath the earth in Quechua cosmology, a realm of the dead and of the roots of the mountains; his images and masks, carved in stone or modeled in clay, stand for his power over that hidden country. In the colonial era his name was pressed into service as the Quechua word for the Christian devil, and the figure was forever blurred in two, ancient lord of the underworld on one side, Christian demon on the other. The ambiguity survives in the festivals of the Andes: at carnival and in the mining towns of Bolivia and Peru dancers wear elaborate Supay masks, and in the tin and silver mines he is courted with coca, cigarettes and chicha as the 'tío,' the uncle of the depths, who both gives the ore and may take the miner. Offerings and images of Supay were and are set out to keep his favor, especially by those who work beneath the earth. The figurine thus carries a double history, of the pre-Christian dead and of the devil the priests once taught.
source: Andean oral tradition and colonial records

name: Pishtaco Knife
era: Andean folk belief to the present
powers: Cuts fat from the living to sell it in secret.
description: The knife of the Pishtaco is the blade of the fat-stealer of the Andes, a figure who is said to creep upon sleeping travelers or the unwary on lonely roads and cut the fat from their bodies to sell it in secret, for candles, soap or, in the modern telling, to be shipped abroad for machines. The weapon is rarely seen; it is more feared than described, and a whistle or a shadow at the roadside is enough to raise the terror of the nakaq, as the same figure is called in Quechua. The belief is rooted in the real dread of the stranger and of the outsider, and historians note that it attached itself successively to Spanish priests, colonial officials, and later to police, missionaries and foreign aid workers, whichever authority the community distrusted. The knife is the visible edge of that fear, and stories of the Pishtaco circulate widely across Peru and Bolivia even today. It is one of the clearest cases in South American folklore of a weapon whose power lies not in its edge but in the story that hides behind it.
source: Andean folk belief and regional studies

name: Zemi (Taino Effigy)
material: Carved wood, stone, bone or cotton
powers: Houses a spirit and speaks through the behique.
description: The zemi is the carved effigy through which the Taíno of the Greater Antilles kept their spirits close: figures of wood, stone, bone or cotton, shaped by carvers to hold a spirit and kept in the household, in the fields, or in the house of the cacique. The behique, the ritual specialist, consulted them for health, harvests and answers, and Spanish accounts describe caciques who owned great numbers of them, receiving the first fruits and offering cures before them. Some zemis were consulted in the cohoba ceremony, when the behique inhaled the powder of the sacred seeds and spoke the spirit's words, and a few wooden examples survive from the islands, carved with crouching human forms and small cavities for offerings. The word zemi names both the spirit itself and the object that houses it, so the effigy is the spirit given a body. Today they are prized museum pieces and a central symbol of Taíno heritage in Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic.
source: Colonial accounts and surviving Taino objects

name: Vejigante Mask
material: Papier-mâché with horns, fangs and bright colors
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Scares away evil with its horns and colors at carnival.
description: The vejigante mask of Ponce, Puerto Rico, is a carnival face of papier-mâché crowned with horns, given fangs, bulging eyes and brilliant colors, worn by the vejigante, the trickster of the Puerto Rican Carnival who whirls through the crowds chasing children and driving off evil spirits. The tradition fuses the Spanish festival, the word comes from vejiga, 'bladder,' after the dried bladders the first celebrants carried, with African and Taíno elements, and each town gave the figure its own face. Ponce's masks are the most elaborate, built up with wings and bristling horns; in Loíza the vejigante instead wears a horned mask of coconut or wire and a costume of layered, fluttering cloth. The craft passed from the great twentieth-century mask-makers of the Ponce families to a generation of folk artists, and the careta is now collected as serious Puerto Rican art. At carnival time the masks still roar, horned and laughing, at the heart of the island's most exuberant festival.
source: Puerto Rican carnival tradition

name: Asson
material: Gourd rattle with snake vertebrae and beads
era: Haitian Vodou tradition to the present
powers: Rings the spirits into the peristyle at ceremony.
description: The asson is the sacred rattle of Haitian Vodou, a gourd fitted with a handle and wrapped in a beaded net threaded with snake vertebrae, held only by the houngan or the mambo, the priest and priestess who lead the congregation. Its sound opens the ceremony: as the rattle is shaken before the peristyle, the lwa, the spirits, are called into the space, and its rhythm marks the moment they descend to possess the faithful. The beads are strung in the colors of the spirits, white for Damballah, the great serpent, black and red for Legba, yellow for Kouzen Zaka, and the gourd is kept consecrated, rubbed with red palm oil and cinnamon so that it grows dark and glossy with use. The asson is given to the priest only at the end of a long initiation, and handling another's asson is a grave offense; a related instrument, the chacha, serves the Petro rites. The rattle is thus the credential and the voice of the priest, the object that rings the spirits into the world of the living.
source: Haitian Vodou practice and ethnographic studies

name: Govi
era: Haitian Vodou tradition to the present
powers: Holds the spirits of the ancestors and the dead.
description: The govi is the earthenware jar of Haitian Vodou that holds the presence of the dead, a red clay vessel or bottle kept in the temple where it contains a spirit or the reclaimed spirit of an ancestor. The most solemn use of the govi belongs to the rite of reclamation, when, a year and a day after a death, the priest retrieves the gwobonanj, the 'big guardian angel,' from the waters of Ginen, the abyssal homeland of the spirits, and the wete mò nan dlo ceremony settles it into the jar. The vessel is then fed with offerings, manje mò, food for the dead, and becomes the place where the ancestor may be consulted, giving advice and protection to the living. If the rite fails or the govi is neglected, misfortune is said to follow the family. The plain clay jar is made extraordinary by the ritual that fills it, and its handling is governed by the strictest respect. Through the govi, the family of the living and the world beneath remain one household.
source: Haitian Vodou practice and ethnographic studies

name: Batá Drum
material: Carved hardwood with animal hide heads
era: Cuban Santería tradition to the present
powers: Talks the language of the orishas at ceremony.
description: The batá is the consecrated drum of Cuban Santería, an hourglass-shaped instrument with two heads of different sizes, played in a set of three, the small okónkolo, the middle itótele and the great iyá, the mother drum that speaks the lead voices. The drums descend from the Yoruba bata of West Africa, carried to Cuba by enslaved people and kept alive behind the Catholic saints, and their rhythms are said to speak the language of the orishas during ceremonies, each rhythm belonging to a particular spirit. A consecrated batá has the orisha Añá installed within it, and only initiated male drummers, omo Añá, may play it; the drums are never allowed to touch the ground and are fed and dressed when not in use. Changó, the thunder deity, is held to be the drums' spiritual owner. The iyá leads and the smaller drums answer, and together they call the orishas down into the gathering; beyond the temple, batá rhythms entered Cuban music and from there the world, but the sacred instrument remains the heart of the religion it serves.
source: Cuban Santería practice and music studies

name: Eleke
material: Beaded necklaces in the colors of the orishas
era: Cuban Santería tradition to the present
powers: Binds the wearer to the protection of a specific orisha.
description: The eleke is the beaded necklace of Cuban Santería, strung in the colors of a particular orisha and given in ceremony to place the wearer under that spirit's protection. White for Obatalá, red and white for Changó, blue and white for Yemayá, yellow for Oshun, the pattern of the beads names the orisha to anyone who knows the tradition, and the necklaces are worn close to the skin as a constant guard. The eleke descends from the beaded collars of Yoruba religion, brought to Cuba with the people who were enslaved and transformed into the religion's regalia; each necklace is consecrated before it is given, and the ceremony of receiving one marks a step into the religion's life. Removing the necklace, or letting it break, is treated with concern, and the beads are handled respectfully and kept clean. The eleke is thus at once ornament, devotion and a visible map of the sacred.
source: Cuban Santería practice and ethnographic studies

name: Duho
powers: Raises the cacique above the ground and close to the spirits.
description: The duho is the carved wooden seat of the Taíno, a low ceremonial stool of guaiacum or mahogany on which caciques and behiques sat in ritual, carved in the shape of an animal, a crouching figure or a reclining zemi with upturned chin and closed eyes. Spanish chroniclers recorded chiefs receiving Columbus and his men seated on duhos, and surviving museum pieces dated to around AD 600 span the islands from Cuba to the Bahamas, showing the form was ancient and widespread. The stool lifted its sitter above the ground and toward the spirits, and it was used in the cohoba ceremony, when the behique inhaled the sacred powder and entered a visionary state; some duhos are carved with a flat surface that could support a tray or zemi during those rites. The finest are praised for the grace of their carving, with four legs and a curved back shaped from a single piece of wood. The duho is one of the most distinctive objects of Taíno art and a proud emblem of Caribbean Indigenous heritage.
source: Archaeological duhos in museum collections and early colonial accounts

name: Lechuguilla Mask
powers: Worn at the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes to escape King Herod.
description: The lechuguilla is the masked costume of the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes in Hatillo, Puerto Rico, held every December 28, when costumed runners race through the streets of the town in painted wire-mesh masks and gowns covered in ruffled fabric curls. The celebration descends from a custom brought by the Canary Island settlers who founded Hatillo in 1823, and it re-enacts the biblical Massacre of the Innocents: the masked runners, called corredores, take the part of King Herod's soldiers, hunting the Christ child, while the crowd flees and turns the hunt into a chase of laughter. The masks, made of cedazo wire covered in papier-mâché and painted in bright colors, are the work of local artisans, and the whole costume is often finished with a crown of fabric flowers or ribbons. Though the name lechuguilla is only partly explained, in Puerto Rico the same word names an aquatic plant, the festival itself is one of the island's most beloved traditions, a December carnival that has run for two centuries.
source: Puerto Rican festival tradition

name: Qulliq
material: Carved soapstone with a moss or cotton wick
powers: The woman's light and warmth that held the igloo together.
description: The qulliq is the crescent-shaped soapstone lamp of the Inuit, burned with seal oil and a wick of moss or Arctic cotton, the only source of light and heat inside the snow house through the long polar night. It was tended by the women of the household, who trimmed the wick to keep the flame steady, melted snow for drinking water, dried clothes and boots over its warmth, and cooked simple meals beside it; a well-managed flame was a mark of a skilled housewife. The lamp gave the igloo its glow and its life, and the word qulliq itself is the everyday name for light in many Inuit languages. When the hunter returned, the lamp was also the signal of home. Today the qulliq survives as a powerful symbol, lit with ceremony at Inuit gatherings and cultural events, while modern homes keep it as a reminder of a past when a single small flame held a family warm against the polar night.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Ulu
material: Blade of iron or slate with wood, bone or antler handle
powers: The all-purpose blade of the household and the camp.
description: The ulu is the broad-bladed knife of the Inuit and other Arctic peoples, a semicircular blade of slate or iron fitted with a short handle, used by the women of the household for every cutting task of the camp. With its curved edge and its grip held in the whole hand, the ulu lets pressure be applied with the arm, slicing through thick hide, frozen meat and fish with a rocking motion, and it is used for skinning game, trimming skins, cutting food and scraping hides for sewing. The shape is ancient, blades of ground slate have been found in Arctic sites, and it was adapted to steel when trade made metal available; regional forms range from the small knife of fine work to larger blades for heavy hide. The ulu is primarily a woman's tool and a symbol of the household's life, and it remains in use across the North today, with modern steel versions sold and used alongside traditional ones. Its quiet usefulness made it, with the qulliq, one of the two essential tools of the Arctic home.
source: Inuit tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Kayak
material: Sealskin stretched over a wood or bone frame
powers: Carries its hunter silently across the open sea after seals.
description: The kayak is the one-man hunting boat of the Inuit, Yupik and Inupiat, a frame of wood or bone stretched tight with sealskin, so light and watertight that a single hunter could carry it, launch it alone, and paddle it silently across the open sea after seals, walrus and whales. The hunter sat in its small cockpit, wearing a skin parka lashed to the rim so that the boat sealed around him, and with his harpoon and lance he could hunt from the surface and even right the kayak in the Eskimo roll, turning it over and back with a twist of the paddle. The design was perfected over millennia and was one of the Arctic inventions that explorers and missionaries carried back to the world, giving the English word kayak from the Inuktitut qajaq. In legend the boat carries its own weight too: in the tale of Sedna, the sea mother, her father rows her out over the water in his kayak before she becomes the ruler of the sea beasts. The kayak remains a living Arctic boat, rebuilt in traditional materials for festivals and races.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic maritime records

name: Amauti
material: Caribou skin with a large back hood
powers: Carries a baby in warmth against its mother's back.
description: The amauti is the woman's parka of the Inuit, cut from caribou skin with a large hood and a deep pouch across the back, the amaut, in which a baby rides warm against its mother's body. The pouch lets the child nurse and sleep without being lifted into the cold, while the hood shields mother and child together from the wind, and the whole garment is sewn with the legendary precision of Inuit women, who cut and stitch by eye so that the seams shed weather. A well-made amauti is a work of both craft and love, the fit of the pouch, the length of the tails, the fur trim at the hood's edge are all judged by the women who wear them. The garment is so central to Arctic motherhood that its making was a skill passed from mother to daughter over generations. Today the amauti is still worn in the North, and contemporary Inuit designers have carried its shape into modern fashion as a proud mark of identity.
source: Inuit tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Tupilak
material: Carved bone, ivory, antler or stone
powers: A vengeful spirit assembled to harm an enemy.
description: The tupilak is a spirit figure of the Greenlandic Inuit, assembled by an angakkuq, a shaman, from the parts of animals, bone, skin, hair and sinew, sometimes joined with the remains of a dead child, and given life through ritual chants so that it could be sent against an enemy. The tupilak was cast into the sea and swam to its victim, but the magic was dangerous in both directions: if the victim proved stronger, the spirit was said to turn back on its maker, and only a public confession could break its power. Because the figures were made from perishable matter, none of the true tupilak survive, and the ritual was feared more than seen. In the early twentieth century carvers began making grotesque figures from walrus ivory, whale tooth, wood and caribou antler, and the tupilak became a celebrated form of Greenlandic art, sold across the world. The carvings carry the old menace into the gallery, part talisman and part monster.
source: Greenlandic oral tradition and ethnographic records

name: Harpoon
material: Wood shaft with toggle-head of bone or ivory
powers: Strikes the seal and holds it even as the line plays out.
description: The harpoon of the Inuit is the throwing weapon perfected for the open sea, a wooden shaft fitted with a detachable head of bone or ivory that buries itself in the seal's hide and toggles, turning beneath the skin so the animal cannot tear free as the line plays out. The hunter cast from the kayak, holding the line so that the wounded seal could be hauled in as it tired, and the same principle was scaled up with heavier heads and floats for walrus and whales. The design is one of the great achievements of Arctic engineering, refined over millennia of open-water hunting, and it was among the tools that European whalers and explorers adopted and copied. In the belief of the Inuit, the success of the hunt was bound to the goodwill of the sea mother Sedna, who released the animals to a hunter who honored her; a harpoon cast without that favor was said to come back empty. The toggle-head harpoon remains a symbol of the Arctic hunter's skill and restraint.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Ade (Yoruba Beaded Crown)
material: Glass beads, velvet or cotton cloth, seed beads
description: The ade is the beaded crown of the Yoruba oba, the king, a cone- or basket-shaped headdress whose cascading fringe of glass beads veils the wearer's face, leaving only the mouth visible as he speaks. The patterns worked in the beads are a language of their own: birds, the Ogboni eye, the royal face, and motifs recalling Oduduwa, the founding ancestor from whom the kingship descends, whose divine gaze the veil is said to shield his subjects from. The crown is worn only at the most solemn moments, enthronement, annual festivals, the great ceremonies of the palace, and when a king dies his ade is buried or retired with him, for the crown is not the ruler's property but the office's. Coronation is unthinkable without it, and the beadwork, done by the royal artisans, may take months for a single crown. In the diaspora the ade has become the emblem of Yoruba monarchy and of the dignity of the ancestral religion.
source: Yoruba coronation tradition; museum collections (British Museum, Musée du quai Branly)

name: Oshe Shango Dance Wand
powers: Said to channel Shango's lightning and to summon or cool his wrath in dance.
description: The oshe is the carved wooden dance wand of the Yoruba Shango cult, its upper end shaped into a double-bladed axe, the emblem of Shango, the god of thunder and lightning. Dancers of the cult swing paired oshe during worship, and the axe is said to carry the deity's power: the flash of the blade is his lightning, the heft of the wood his strength, and the double edge his two faces of destruction and renewal. Older examples are carved with a face of the deity or of a priestess, and the wand is kept on the shrine and treated with respect, often touched to the ground before the dance begins. The oshe is danced at festivals, at the great ceremonies of the Shango priests, and wherever the thunder god is honored, and the carving tradition is among the best known of Yoruba art. The wand thus speaks without words, holding in a single object the whole theology of the storm.
source: Yoruba Shango cult tradition; museum examples

name: Opon Ifa Divination Board
description: The opon ifa is the round wooden tray on which the Yoruba babalawo, the priest of divination, reads the will of the orisha Orunmila: dusted with wood powder, the tray receives the patterns traced as the diviner casts the palm nuts or swings the divination chain and interprets the emerging odu. The rim of the tray is carved with the face of Eshu, the messenger who carries the signs, and with figures of proverb scenes, and the flat face is kept smooth so the powder can be drawn and redrawn again and again through the reading. The tray is treated as sacred: it is never set directly on the ground, only the initiated handle it, and after each consultation the powder is gathered and the board cleaned with ceremony. The opon ifa is the visible center of Ifa divination, the system that has guided Yoruba families for centuries and has since spread with the diaspora to the Americas. In its carvings and its signs it holds the memory of a people.
source: Ifa divination tradition; oral knowledge of the babalawo

name: Ikenga Shrine Figure
powers: Embodies the owner's personal achievement, strength, and right hand.
description: The ikenga is the carved wooden shrine figure of Igbo men, a seated human form with curving horns, a sword and a carved knife held in its hands, standing on the family altar as the image of its owner's achievement and strength. The figure represents the owner's chi, his personal spirit of accomplishment, and the horned head recalls the ram and the aggressive power of the ancestor-hero; when a man prospered, his ikenga was washed, oiled and given offerings, and when he failed or fell, the figure might be cast away. The right hand, in Igbo thought the hand of action, is honored in the ikenga's upraised arm, and the figure is bound up with the owner's own commitment to strive, the word itself carrying the sense of personal strength. Ikenga are carved in many sizes, from small household figures to great ritual sculptures, and they are among the most recognizable of Igbo arts. They remain in use in the shrine houses of Igboland today.
source: Igbo household tradition; museum collections

name: Gelede Mask
description: The Gelede mask is a carved wooden headdress of the Yoruba, worn tilted on the top of the head by a dancer who gazes out through the costume's veil while the crest rises above him, bearing figures of animals, people, market scenes or the faces of those being honored. The performance honors the great mothers, awon iya wa, 'our mothers,' the powerful women, both living and of the night, whose spiritual force underlies the community, and the dance at once celebrates them and gently mocks the follies of the town, using laughter to restore harmony. Gelede belongs especially to the Yoruba of southwestern Nigeria and spreads across the border into Benin and Togo, and in 2008 UNESCO inscribed it on the list of intangible cultural heritage. The Efe, the night performance that precedes the daytime Gelede, carries the weight of the ritual, with its songs of praise and warning. The masks, painted in bright colors, are the festive and formidable face of that whole tradition.
source: Yoruba oral tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listing of Gelede

name: Edan Ogboni Staff
era: Traditional, still used in society rites
powers: Held to enforce truth and justice, sealing oaths made before the earth's authority.
description: The edan are paired staffs of brass or iron belonging to the Ogboni, or Osugbo, the elders' society of the Yoruba, each staff topped by a seated human figure, one male and one female, joined by a short length of chain. The pair stands for the moral unity of the earth, and the edan is kept on the society's altar, where oaths are sworn over it; to swear falsely while the edan rested before the assembly was to call down the earth's judgment. The society, whose name means 'elders,' served as the council of justice and the keeper of the land's authority, and its emblem carried that weight. Members wear small edan hung about the neck as badges of office, while the great pair on the altar is used in the society's rites. The figures are cast by the brassworkers and kept polished, and the edan remains one of the most distinctive objects of Yoruba governance. It joins the sacred and the legal in a single staff of iron.
source: Ogboni society tradition; British Museum collections

name: Benin Bronze Plaque
maker: Igbesanmwan guild casters of the Igun quarter
description: The Benin bronzes are the cast-brass plaques that once covered the pillars of the Oba's palace in the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, depicting the king, his warriors, chiefs and courtiers in high relief against openwork backgrounds. They were made by the guild of the Igun quarter using lost-wax casting, a craft reserved for the palace, and they record royal history, court protocol, the regalia of office and even the Portuguese visitors who came to the coast in the sixteenth century. In 1897 a British punitive expedition took the city, looted the palace and carried thousands of objects to Europe, where they entered museums from London to Berlin; the word bronze is traditional, but most of the plaques are brass, an alloy of copper and zinc. The plaques have since become the center of one of the world's great restitution debates, as Nigeria and the museums negotiate their return. They remain masterpieces of African cast metalwork and a record of a kingdom that Europeans both traded with and destroyed.
source: British Museum collections; Edo court history and restitution scholarship

name: The Golden Stool (Sika Dwa)
powers: Holds the soul (sunsum) of the Asante nation; its wellbeing is the nation's wellbeing.
description: The Sika Dwa, the Golden Stool of the Asante, is a gold-covered wooden stool kept unseated upon as the soul, the sunsum, of the Asante nation, the supreme emblem of its sovereignty. Tradition holds that in the late seventeenth century the priest Okomfo Anokye called it down from the sky, and it settled onto the lap of the first king, Osei Tutu, proving his divine right; since then the stool has never been allowed to touch the ground, and a blackened stool commemorates each departed king. When a British governor demanded the stool in 1900, the Asante rose in the war led by the queen mother Yaa Asantewaa, choosing to fight rather than surrender their nation's soul. The stool sits on its own stool, sheltered in the palace at Kumasi, and is brought out only on the greatest occasions. Its history joins the spiritual, the political and the martial in a single object of wood and gold.
source: Asante oral tradition; Manhyia Palace Museum

name: Akan Goldweight (Abrammuo)
description: The Akan goldweight, the abrammuo, is a small cast-brass piece used from the fifteenth century onward to weigh gold dust in the trade of present-day Ghana, one of the great mercantile tools of the Atlantic world. The weights were cast by the lost-wax method, and the figurative ones depict animals, people, proverbs, objects and scenes of daily life in miniature, each one with a story to tell. The art of the weights lay in the proverb: a man could hand his companion a weight of a crocodile with a bird, and the pair would 'speak' the proverb it illustrated, making the weights a language in the marketplace. They were kept in carved boxes or purses with brass spoons and balances, and their quality was judged by law, with penalties for false weights. Collectors prize them as sculpture, but they began as everyday instruments of commerce. The goldweight joins trade, law and orature into a single small object.
source: Akan trade tradition; museum collections (British Museum)

name: Kente Cloth
description: Kente is the strip-woven cloth of the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana, built up from narrow bands of silk and cotton woven on narrow looms and sewn edge to edge into bold geometric patterns, each of which has a name and a proverb meaning. Weaving was traditionally a male craft tied to the royal court, and particular patterns were reserved for the king; the colors carry their own language, with gold for royalty, green for growth, red for passion or danger, and the cloth is worn for the great occasions of Akan life. The Asante origin tradition credits the spider Anansi with teaching the first weavers, and the name kente comes from the Akan word for the open basket that the patterns recall. Kwame Nkrumah wore kente at Ghana's independence, and the cloth has become a worldwide emblem of African identity, worn by leaders and diaspora communities alike. Every strip of kente is woven memory, pattern by pattern.
source: Asante oral tradition

name: Adinkra Cloth
material: Cotton, carved calabash stamps, tree-bark dye
description: Adinkra is the stamped cloth of the Akan, dyed in dark tones and printed with the symbolic motifs that bear the same name, each one carrying a proverb and a moral lesson: the sankofa bird that looks back to learn, gye nyame, 'except God,' and dozens more that together form a written language in cloth. The dye is made from the bark of the badie tree, boiled down to a deep black, and the blocks are carved from calabash, pressed into the fabric to stamp the patterns row by row. The cloth was traditionally worn at funerals and by the bereaved, its dark ground expressing mourning while the symbols spoke of the virtues of the dead, and it is still made at the great adinkra center of Ntonso in Ghana. Today the symbols have spread far beyond the cloth, appearing in architecture, jewelry and design, but the textile remains the root of the tradition. Adinkra cloth is wisdom made wearable.
source: Akan oral tradition; museum collections

name: Fon Asen Altar Staff
description: The asen is the commemorative altar staff of the Fon of Benin, a forged iron pole topped with a figurative scene, an ancestor at work, an animal, a scene of daily life, set in a base of clay or iron and placed beside the ancestor altar of the compound. When a family member dies, an asen is raised for the dead, and through it the ancestor receives offerings during the rites of remembrance and is fed and spoken with as if still present. The iron is worked by smiths, who are themselves set apart in Fon society, and the figures are made to be read: a hunter with his gun, a woman at the mortar, the emblems of the life the dead one lived. The asen is central to the Vodun practice of ancestor veneration, and older pieces, their iron darkened with age and offerings, are valued in museums as records of Dahomey's families. In the compound, the row of asen is the visible genealogy of the household.
source: Fon ancestor ritual; museum collections (Musée du quai Branly)

name: Zangbeto Masquerade Costume
description: The zangbeto is the towering masquerade of the Fon of Benin, a cone-shaped costume of plaited straw and raffia worn over the body so that only a skirt of fibers is seen, with the performer hidden inside making the figure spin, whirl and race through the streets of its own accord. The word means 'night watchman,' and the zangbeto is exactly that: the masked guardian of the town that patrols after dark, hunting witches and thieves, and every village has its zangbeto society with its initiates and its rules. The costume is never empty, the spirit is said to enter it, and the figure dances, chants and admonishes the crowd, keeping the peace through a mixture of awe and discipline. The zangbeto is rooted in the Vodun religion of southern Benin and Togo, where it protects the community and judges wrongdoers. When the straw figure spins in the dark, the line between costume and spirit is meant to be forgotten.
source: Fon oral tradition

name: Dahomey Applique Cloth
description: Dahomey applique is the court textile of the Fon, a rectangular cloth of cotton on which cut-out cloth figures are sewn to record royal history and proverb: kings, warriors, the kingdom's celebrated women soldiers, animals and scenes of triumph, each figure placed in a tableau that tells a story at a glance. The cloths were commissioned for the royal court of Abomey and were carried as banners and hung as umbrella covers in the great processions, where the king's deeds marched before him in fabric. The leading artisans were the kings' own embroiderers, and the tradition was passed down in workshops that still practice it in Abomey today, now serving collectors and museums as well as the court. Every figure is a word: the king appears as a buffalo or a lion, enemies as the animals that were felled, so the cloth is read like a text. Dahomey applique carries the memory of a kingdom in colored cloth.
source: Fon court tradition; museum collections (Musée du quai Branly)

name: Dogon Kanaga Mask
description: The kanaga is the wooden headdress of the Dogon of Mali, a crest of crossed bars rising from a vertical plank, danced by the men of the masked society at the dama, the great funeral rites that lead the souls of the dead to their ancestors. The mask is worn on the top of the head, the dancer looking out through the costume as the double cross revolves, and its form is read as the structure of the world, the arms of the cross as the sky and the earth, or as the hand of the creator god Amma shaping the cosmos. Every sixty years the Sigui, the great regeneration ceremony, renews the tradition, and the masks mediate between the living and the dead, banishing the souls gently from the village. The Dogon are famous for the depth of their cosmology, studied by ethnographers since the 1930s, and the kanaga has become the emblem of that tradition in African art. In dance the mask sets the universe spinning.
source: Dogon masked society tradition; ethnographic studies (Griaule school)

name: Chiwara Headdress
description: The chiwara is the antelope headdress of the Bamana of Mali, a carved figure with a long neck, elegant horns and an openwork body, danced in pairs at the agricultural festivals in honor of the mythic being who, the Bamana say, taught humanity to farm. The dance re-enacts the teaching: the headdresses are tied to a cap on the heads of two dancers who leap and crouch like antelopes feeding, while the rest of the village raises the hoe to the rhythm. The long horns curve toward the sun, and the zigzag crest on the back of the older style recalls the sun's rays falling on the fields; two forms are recognized, the vertical style of the north and the horizontal style of the south. The chiwara is not worshiped but honored, it is the remembered teacher of agriculture, and the dance gives thanks for the gift. Today the headdress is among the best-known of African sculptures, though it is still danced at sowing time in the Bamana villages.
source: Bamana oral tradition

name: Bogolanfini Mud Cloth
description: Bogolanfini, the mud cloth of the Bamana of Mali, is a cotton textile painted by women with a dye of fermented river mud, worked over a yellow ground to leave dark geometric patterns that record proverbs, clan histories and the teachings of initiation. The cloth is made in a slow sequence: the cotton is washed and dyed with a yellow infusion of leaves, then the designs are drawn in mud, which reacts with the yellow to leave a deep brown-black as the background is rinsed away. The cloths were worn at initiations, by hunters, and by women at the turning points of life, and the patterns are held to protect the wearer and to carry the memory of the family. Since the 1980s bogolan has left the village for the fashion world, worn by Malian musicians and designers and celebrated as a national art. Each bolt of bogolanfini is a document of the society that made it, written in earth.
source: Bamana women's tradition
